info.bio: Trece años después de su nacimiento como banda, Sloan no sólo siguen juntos, sino que además acaban de preparar una recopilación de sus mejores canciones. La fina ironía que envuelve el asunto no es que la banda no se lo merezca –siguen siendo tan aclamados y queridos como en sus comienzos –, sino que sólo unos pocos, quizás ni siquiera ellos mismos, pensaron que llegarían al año 2005 intactos y sin bajas en su formación original, además de enfrentarse al reto de editar una antología de sus singles.

scenes.name: Más ruidoso que el rock: noise-rock de los noventa
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: En los noventa los géneros de los ochenta (lo-fi, industrial, gótico, roots-rock, noise-rock, indie-pop, techno, ambient) se separan en lugar de fundirse: es la revancha de «la provincia» (el Sur, Seattle) y la década con menos géneros nuevos (grunge, post-rock, trip-hop, drum'n'bass, glitch). La influencia de Sonic Youth y Pussy Galore es la más visible: Bewitched, Boss Hog, Jon Spencer Blues Explosion (deconstrucción posmoderna del blues), Versus. El hardcore apocalíptico de Chicago: Jesus Lizard (Goat), Dazzling Killmen, Unsane. Polvo y la escuela de Chapel Hill, Come, Supreme Dicks, Tsunami, Brainiac; en Inglaterra, Gallon Drunk, Jacob's Mouse, Prolapse; en Canadá, la escuela de Halifax (Eric's Trip, Sloan, Jale).

podcast.title: Formation and Longevity (1991)
podcast.body: Sloan was formed in 1991, emerging from the Halifax area music scene after previous bands like Carney Lake Road. They are noted for their exceptional longevity, having existed since their formation. "Sloan. They were formed in 1991."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Formation of Murder Records (Early 1992)
podcast.body: Sloan established their own record label, Murder Records, in early 1992, to release their debut EP "The Peppermint-eaky" and bypass the extended timelines of major labels like Geffen/DGC, which projected a much later release date for their first album. The label allowed them to quickly put out music, facilitate touring, and later expanded to release records for other Halifax bands, fostering a communal scene. "So that's why we started murder records was just to put out that EP. And then there was other bands that we knew of that we were friends with."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Post-Twice Removed Breakup Rumors (1995)
podcast.body: In late 1994 and early 1995, rumors of Sloan disbanding spread, culminating in an April 1st, 1995 newswire story. Reasons cited by manager Chip Sutherland included Geffen's perceived inadequate US promotion, Andrew Scott's move to Toronto, and the band's reluctance to continue under a major label contract. Chris Murphy even announced a Halifax show as their last. "After twice removed, things began to, well, they began to fall apart. This was when the breakup rumors started. On April 1st, 1995, a story was carried on the newswire. Sloan disbands Halifax, Grunge Pop's sensation may be calling it quits."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Chart Magazine Accolades (1996)
podcast.body: In 1996, Chart Magazine declared "Twice Removed" the number one Canadian album of all time and "Underwhelmed" the number two Canadian song of all time, signifying significant critical acclaim within Canada. "Chart Magazine named twice removed as the number one Canadian album of all time. And underwhelmed was picked as the number two Canadian song of all time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Juno Award (1996)
podcast.body: Sloan won a Juno Award in 1996, recognizing their contributions to Canadian music, around the time of their album "One Chord to Another." "They wanted Juneau, Chart Magazine named twice removed as the number one Canadian album of all time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: The Enclave Record Deal (1996)
podcast.body: After departing Geffen, Sloan signed with The Enclave in 1996, a short-lived "boutique label with tons of money" founded by Tom Zutat, mentor to Todd Sullivan. Zutat aimed to make Sloan a major hit, but the label went out of business within six months, leaving Sloan without a US label by 1997. "And we signed to this other label called the OnClave, which was short lived, which just set up to be really good at head, like balance of bastion, like the water boys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: All Members Contribute Songs and Vocals
podcast.body: Sloan is noted for its unique collaborative structure where every member of the band not only gets a turn at the microphone for lead vocals but also contributes songs to their albums. "not only does everyone get a turn at the mic, but everyone in the band also gets to contribute songs"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Second Voice

podcast.title: American Market Attempts
podcast.body: Sloan made multiple efforts to break into the lucrative American market. Their first attempt was in 1992 with the "Smeared" album on Geffen, Nirvana's label, but it fell apart due to label politics. A mid-1990s deal with The Enclave also failed when the label went out of business. Even in 2003, they tried again, managing only about two appearances on MTV's "120 Minutes." "Yes, we never had any kind of, you know, we were on 120 minutes on MTV in the States."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Andrew Scott - Athletic and Charismatic
podcast.body: Andrew Scott was a provincial track and field record holder in Nova Scotia before joining Sloan as the drummer. He was also voted one of Canada's 20 sexiest musicians. "And drummer Andrew Scott was the former holder of several provincial track and field records in Nova Scotia. He was also voted one of Canada's 20 sexiest musicians."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Aspiration for International Recognition and Box Sets
podcast.body: Despite feeling they hadn't "gotten any bigger" in 1999, Sloan continues to record with the long-term goal of accumulating an "enormous body of work." They hope to eventually gain recognition from international publications like Mojo Magazine or Record Collector Magazine, which could lead to a retrospective box set and coffee table book, although they acknowledge the audience might currently be too small without a "huge hit." "Just to have an enormous body of work so that Mojo Magazine finally goes, we are sorry, we never wrote about you guys and you guys are unbelievable and you have all this stuff and nobody knows."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Band Name Origin
podcast.body: The band's name, "Sloan," was derived from the nickname of Jason Larson, the bass player of the New Brunswick/Bedford band The Straight Jackets. Larson's French-speaking boss in a Montreal warehouse mispronounced "Slow One" as "Sloan," and the band adopted this nickname, featuring Larson's face on their debut EP, "The Peppermint-eaky." "Their bass player, his nickname, he worked... And his French boss used to call... The bass player, Jason Larson used to call him Slow One. And with the French accent, it just turned into Sloan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Canada's Answer to Nirvana
podcast.body: Sloan, from Halifax, was initially perceived as "Canada's answer to Nirvana," leading to Halifax being briefly considered "Seattle East" due to the widespread frenzy and saturation of grunge. "Sloan originally pegged as Canada's answer to Nirvana. And for a short while, Halifax was considered to be Seattle East."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 3: Grunge

podcast.title: Canadian Band Challenges
podcast.body: Operating as a rock band in Canada, the world's second-largest country, presents unique challenges due to its vast geography (nearly 10 million square kilometers spread over six time zones with just over three people per square kilometer). Touring bands become intimately familiar with the 7,604 kilometers of the Trans-Canada Highway. Despite 77% of the population living in cities, bands must work extremely hard to reach fans, especially while living next door to the largest net exporter of popular culture in the universe, the United States, which has "chewed up the domestic careers of countless bands." "Geography has chewed up the domestic careers of countless bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Chris Murphy - Child Modeling Career
podcast.body: As a child, Chris Murphy modeled Winnie the Pooh sleeping bags for the Eaton's catalog and appeared in Snyder's Bacon commercials, where he played a child stealing bacon. This early experience is humorously compared to Eddie Vedder's own child modeling. "It was Chris. I did as a kid. I modeled Winnie the Pooh sleeping bag. Well, I was in the, like, the Eaton's in the series catalog. I know a couple of commercials. It's Snyder's Bacon."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Collaborated with Weezer
podcast.body: The guys from Sloan collaborated with Weezer on the album "Ratitude," though their contributions were uncredited and recorded in 2003. "And the guys from Sloan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rivers Cuomo and Weezer - Alt-Rock's Nerd Heroes Part 2

podcast.title: Collaborative and Individualistic Songwriting
podcast.body: Sloan operates with an egalitarian approach where all four members sing, write, and contribute creatively, splitting money equally. Andrew Scott's move to Toronto in 1993 fostered a more individualistic recording process, with members often playing all instruments on their own songs. This "parallel play" style was particularly evident on their album of the same name. "So we've all kind of evolved into this band that writes sort of individually."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Contractual Standoff with Geffen
podcast.body: Facing a six-album contract with Geffen after their informal breakup, Sloan initially withheld the news from the label to avoid disadvantageous "broken up band" contractual clauses. Geffen eventually released them from their contract in an artist-friendly move, allowing Sloan to pursue other options. "As a band that was broken up, we were on Geffen and we were signed something like six records or something like that, which is not really in our favor."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Cult Phenomenon in the States
podcast.body: Despite limited mainstream success in the United States, Sloan has achieved a "cult phenomenon" status there. American fans typically discover them from their college days when "Smeared" was on Geffen, or through independent research online, appreciating their pop and rock music. This underground following becomes "more and more underground" the further south one travels. "So we are a cult phenomenon in the States, which is fun. But we make our money in Canada because we benefit from mainstream media and stuff like that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Democratic Band Structure
podcast.body: Sloan operates with an "uber democratic structure" where every member writes songs and sings lead vocals. All money is split equally among the four members, which has been crucial in keeping the band together and avoiding the conflicts over financial distribution that have plagued other bands, such as The Smiths. "Every single member of Sloan writes songs and every single member gets a chance to sing lead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Desire for Critical Acclaim
podcast.body: Chris Murphy jokingly expressed a long-term goal for Sloan to amass an "enormous body of work" in hopes that prestigious publications like Mojo Magazine or Record Collector Magazine would eventually acknowledge their extensive discography. He envisions a future box set and coffee table book, but only if a "huge hit" makes it financially viable for a larger audience. "Just to have an enormous body of work so that Mojo Magazine finally goes, we are sorry. We never wrote about you guys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Domestic Focus and Longevity
podcast.body: Sloan has primarily operated as a domestic act in Canada since 1991, running their own label and partnering with larger distributors. They have consistently adapted to the music business's challenges, maintaining their band with zero lineup changes, a feat that is considered "pretty remarkable." "A Canadian band who has worked mainly as a domestic act since 1991, running their own label, working deals with other bigger labels to distribute their stuff, and surviving everything in music business has thrown at them with zero lineup changes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Early 1990s Prime Time Success
podcast.body: Sloan was among the Canadian bands that got "a shot at prime time" in the early 1990s. "There was Pluto and Jail and Doeboys and Rusty and Sloan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 8: The CanRock Revolution

podcast.title: Early Career Success
podcast.body: Sloan initiated their fruitful multi-decade career in the very late 1980s or early 1990s, establishing themselves as a significant band during the Canadian music boom. They are regarded as one of the enduring stars from that period. "Sloan...had fruitful multi-decade careers that began in either the very late 1980s or the early 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the '90s: Part 1

podcast.title: Evolution of Songwriting
podcast.body: Since Andrew Scott moved to Toronto in 1993, the band's collaborative process evolved, encouraging individual members to sing, write, and creatively contribute independently. This approach, combined with equal money splitting, has been key to the band's longevity and cohesion. "So we've all kind of evolved into this band that writes sort of individually."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Featured in "In Their Own Words" Series
podcast.body: Sloan was the first band to be featured in the "In Their Own Words" series, which aims to bring multiple band members into the studio to share their personal history. "Sloan was first..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding Members' Diverse Backgrounds
podcast.body: The band's members brought diverse backgrounds to its formation: Jay Ferguson was a record store clerk from Halifax; Chris Murphy was a child model for Winnie the Pooh sleeping bags and Snyder's Bacon commercials; Andrew Scott was a provincial high school high jump champion and track and field record holder, later voted one of Canada's 20 sexiest musicians; and Patrick Pentland was born in Northern Ireland, lived in Jamaica, and settled in Sackville, Nova Scotia. "And this is a show on how a record store clerk, a saxophone player born in Northern Ireland, a former provincial high school high jump champion, and a model for Winnie the Pooh sleeping bags in the Eaton's catalog came together to become one of this country's most enduring rock bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Halifax Music Community Support
podcast.body: After gaining major label attention, Sloan made a conscious effort to support the Halifax music scene, where they felt they "knew everybody who was into cool music." They expanded Murder Records to release albums by local bands like Eric's Trip, Hardship Post, and Thrush Hermit, and brought these bands on tour to share opportunities. "But we really tried to be gracious about it and really try part of the expanding murder records and putting out other records was an effort to be a part of the community where we were all of a sudden our aspirations changed to being national or international."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Halifax Roots
podcast.body: Sloan originated from Halifax, Nova Scotia. The title of their 1999 album, "Between the Bridges," directly references the Macdonald and McKay bridges in the municipality, signifying their deep connection to their hometown. "Sloan is originally from Halifax, and there are two main bridges in the municipality."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Internal Competition and Ego
podcast.body: Despite their democratic and egalitarian financial structure, there is acknowledged competition and ego among the members regarding songwriting and singles. Chris Murphy expressed his happiness about "The Other Man" being released as a single, partly because it was his song and stylistically different, especially after Patrick Pentland had achieved "five or six singles in a row." "Well, as I say, I was playing down my bile, but by the time Patrick had about five or six singles in a row, I was like, I had had it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Jay Ferguson - Record Store Clerk
podcast.body: Before Sloan, Jay Ferguson worked as a record store clerk at a secondhand shop in Halifax. He had been playing music with Chris Murphy since the age of seven. "Jay Ferguson was the record store clerk. It was a secondhand shop at Halifax."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Learning Songs for Tour
podcast.body: Sloan has an unusual approach to preparing for tours, often recording albums with many new songs and then needing to learn them later for live performance. Chris Murphy humorously notes, "most bands know how to play the record. And then they go make the record. But we're opposite. I basically have to go buy the record to learn how to play the album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Love Triangle Rumor
podcast.body: There is an internet rumor suggesting that Sloan's song "The Other Man" is based on a real-life love triangle within the Canadian indie music community, supposedly involving Chris Murphy of Sloan, Andrew Whiteman from Broken Social Scene, and Leslie Feist. "I have heard that this song is based on a real love triangle within the Canadian indie community."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Major Part of Can Rock Revolution
podcast.body: Sloan became and continued to be a major part of the Can Rock Revolution, solidifying their place in Canadian music history through their sustained influence and success. "they would go on to and continue to be a major part of the Can Rock Revolution."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of the 90s CanRock Explosion

podcast.title: Patrick Pentland - International Upbringing and Role Change
podcast.body: Patrick Pentland was born in Northern Ireland, lived in Jamaica, and later settled in Sackville, Nova Scotia. He joined Sloan as a guitar player, leading to Chris Murphy's "demotion" to bass within a year because Pentland was considered a better guitarist. "Patrick Pentland was the guy who was born in Northern Ireland. He also lived in Jamaica before his family finally settled in Sacville, Nova Scotia."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Persistence and Success
podcast.body: Sloan has successfully navigated the challenges of the Canadian music industry, maintaining a solid and respectable living as rock stars. They have developed efficiencies, established a loyal fan base, and perfected their routine since forming in 1991. "They may not be rich, but they are making a solid and respectable living as rock stars in Canada. Sloan is one of those bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Post-Can Rock Revolution Survival
podcast.body: Sloan's career continued successfully long after the 1990s, indicating the enduring impact of the Can Rock Revolution. "Many acts survived long after the decade ended. The tragically hip, Sloan, R80p, Serma Glockland, Tea Party, Matt Good, many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 8: The CanRock Revolution

podcast.title: Recording Philosophy
podcast.body: Chris Murphy prefers making records "on the cheap" to ensure they are seen as a success, prioritizing low cost over high sales figures. He contrasts this with their second album which cost $120,000 due to major label funding, whereas their first record, remixed by Geffen, cost only $1,200. "I like to make everything on the cheap. So that it can be seen as a success."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Regaining Music Rights
podcast.body: Following the collapse of The Enclave and their departure from Geffen, Sloan successfully fought to remain independent and regained the rights to their music. They eventually acquired the Canadian rights to "Smeared" and "Twice Removed," consolidating their entire catalog under their own Murder Records label, a point of pride for the band. "The good news is that Sloan successfully fought to stay independent. They also got the rights to their music back, which, as you heard, is something the band is pretty proud of."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Self-Sufficiency in Recording
podcast.body: After expensive major label experiences (e.g., $120,000 for "Twice Removed"), Sloan embraced self-sufficiency, recording albums like "Never Hear The End of It" and "Parallel Play" in their own rehearsal studio. This allowed them to produce music on a budget, making sales successes easier to achieve. "Why wouldn't we just record it on our practice base?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Signed to Sub Pop
podcast.body: Sloan was signed to Sub Pop for their first album, "Smeared." This significant label signing, coupled with their origin in Halifax, contributed to the city's brief reputation as the "new Seattle" in the early 1990s. "Sloan, from the smeared album of 1992, they would go on to and continue to be a major part of the Can Rock Revolution."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of the 90s CanRock Explosion

podcast.title: Signing to Geffen/DGC Records
podcast.body: Sloan, an indie band from Nova Scotia, signed to Geffen/DGC, Nirvana's record label, after a rapid series of events. A demo tape sent to Cam Carpenter (A&R at MCA Canada) led to a recommendation to Rick Arboit (Network Records), who then passed it to Todd Sullivan (Geffen). Sullivan, impressed by "Underwhelmed," signed them, a rare and exciting occurrence for a Halifax band. "He set it to a friend of his Todd Sullivanic Geffen who loved the song underwhelmed and then came to see his play and then he was like, do you guys want to sign to Geffen?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Unique Album Structure for "Commonwealth"
podcast.body: The 2014 album *Commonwealth*, particularly its vinyl version, is structured as a double album where each of the four sides is dedicated exclusively to material written by a different band member. For instance, Jay Ferguson wrote five tracks for side one, Chris Murphy five for side two, Patrick Pentland four for side three, and Andrew Scott an 18-minute track for side four. "each of the four sides features material written by a member of the band Record one side one features songs by Jay Ferguson five tracks Record one side two is all material from Chris Murphy another five songs Record two side one comes from Patrick Pendland four songs and record two side two is one big long 18-minute track written by Andrew Scott"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Second Voice

podcast.title: Zero Lineup Changes
podcast.body: Since their formation in 1991, Sloan has remarkably maintained the same four members, a testament to their enduring chemistry and "uber democratic structure." This stability is a significant factor in their ability to survive the music business for decades. "Many band who has survived this long in this country with zero lineup changes has got to have some stories."

xref.title: Widespread Cancer and Unsuccessful Treatments (September 1980)
xref.body: After collapsing in Central Park, Bob Marley reported back to the hospital on September 26, 1980, where doctors discovered that the melanoma had spread from his toe to his brain, forming a massive tumor, and also to his liver and lungs. He underwent chemotherapy and radiation treatments at Sloan Kettering Hospital, which caused his dreadlocks to fall out, leading to his wife giving him his first haircut in years. However, these conventional treatments proved ineffective. "doctors reported that the cancer had spread from his toe to his brain. There was a massive tumor. They also found cancer in his liver and lungs." "But the chemo and radiation did not work. There was nothing more they could do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Last Moments Of - Part 1

xref.title: Ricky Wilson's AIDS-Related Illness and Death (October 12, 1985)
xref.body: Ricky Wilson, the guitarist for The B-52s, became the first notable musician to die from AIDS on October 12, 1985, just nine days after actor Rock Hudson's passing. He had been ill since 1983 and experienced severe health issues throughout most of 1985, including Kaposi's sarcoma, infections, and pneumonia. Due to the pervasive stigma associated with AIDS and gay men at the time, Wilson kept his condition private, with his sister and bandmate, Cindy Wilson, only learning of his diagnosis three days before his death. He passed away at Sloan Kettering Hospital in New York at the age of 32. "Ricky Wilson became the first notable musician to die of AIDS."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Bridge to Geffen Records
xref.body: Rick Arboit, working at Network Records, received Sloan's tape from Cam Carpenter and liked it, but his hands were tied regarding signing them to MCA. He then connected them to Todd Sullivan at Geffen, indirectly facilitating Sloan's signing to a major label. "He told his friend Rick Arboit who worked at Network to come, hey, check out this band. He liked our tape. And his hands were tied. I don't think he could do anything in Canada at MCA for us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Can Rock Renaissance Artist
xref.body: Cowboy Junkies are cited as an example of a band whose music falls under the "Can Rock" umbrella, a term describing a "large swath of music created in this country" between 1985 and 1995. "Since its publication, Can Rock has come to describe a large swath of music created in this country, from the tragically hip to Sarah McLaughlin and from Sloan to the cowboy junkies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 8: The CanRock Revolution

xref.title: Chris Murphy's Hiatus Project
xref.body: During Sloan's temporary hiatus after "Twice Removed," Chris Murphy toured with a band called The Super Friends, exploring individual musical endeavors. "Toured with a band called The Super Friends."

xref.title: Co-Manager and Scene Figure
xref.body: Peter Rowan served as a co-manager for Sloan and was also involved in managing other bands from the Halifax scene, such as Eric's Trip and Hardship Post. His connections facilitated Murder Records' expansion to release records for these other local groups. "And also our co-manager, the time Peter Rowan was also involved with managing like Eric's trip and hardship post."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Dominant Radio Sound Contrast
xref.body: The Smashing Pumpkins represented the prevailing "really loud guitars" sound on radio when Sloan recorded "Twice Removed." Sloan consciously chose to diverge from this trend, opting for quieter guitars, a move they considered "career suicide." "And everything that was on radio at that time was smashing pumpkins or just really loud guitars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Career in Thrush Hermit
xref.body: Joel Plaskett (referred to as "Joe Plasket") was a young member of the Halifax band Thrush Hermit, around 16 years old, when they were supported by Sloan through record releases on Murder Records and touring opportunities. "Thrusher mitt. Who gives you Joe Plasket now. Those guys were kids. They were 16 or whatever."

xref.title: External Collaborators and Multiple Producers for Ratitude
xref.body: For "Ratitude," Weezer brought in outside collaborators for the first time, including Jermaine Dupri, members of All-American Rejects, Lil Wayne, Dan Wilson from Semi-Sonic, and the guys from Sloan (though uncredited and parts recorded in 2003). The album also had four producers, including Dr. Luke and Jacknife Lee, plus Rivers Cuomo, totaling five. "For the first time outside collaborators were brought in, including Germain Dupree, a couple of guys from all American rejects, Lil Wayne, Dan Wilson from Semi-Sonic, and the guys from Sloan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rivers Cuomo and Weezer - Alt-Rock's Nerd Heroes Part 2

xref.title: Founder of The Enclave and Todd Sullivan's Mentor
xref.body: Tom Zutat founded The Enclave, a short-lived boutique record label with significant funding, and was the mentor to Todd Sullivan, who signed Sloan to Geffen. Zutat's ambition was to make Sloan a major hit to prove Geffen wrong, but The Enclave ceased operations within six months. "It was Tom Zutat, the guy who was the mentor of Todd Sullivan, who was signed to Geffen originally."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Geffen A&R Who Signed Sloan
xref.body: Todd Sullivan, an A&R at Geffen Records, was introduced to Sloan's music by Rick Arboit. He particularly loved their song "Underwhelmed" and, after seeing them perform, offered them a record deal with Geffen. He later became a mentee of Tom Zutat, founder of The Enclave. "He set it to a friend of his Todd Sullivanic Geffen who loved the song underwhelmed and then came to see his play and then he was like, do you guys want to sign to Geffen?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Halifax Scene Contemporaries and Collaborators
xref.body: Eric's Trip was a band from the Halifax scene, co-managed by Peter Rowan. Sloan viewed them as "cooler" and, through their Murder Records label, released a split seven-inch with them and brought them on tour as part of their effort to support the local music community. "And also our co-manager, the time Peter Rowan was also involved with managing like Eric's trip and hardship post. And we eventually put it there records as well."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Highly Regarded Halifax Live Band
xref.body: Hardship Post was a band from the Halifax scene, co-managed by Peter Rowan, and was highly praised by Sloan members as the "best live band" and "insanely good." Sloan supported them by releasing their records on Murder Records and taking them on tour. "Eric's trip were cooler than us. But no, there were a lot of great bands in this band hardship post. They were the best live band. They were insanely good."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on "Smeared"
xref.body: My Bloody Valentine, a "noisy pop" band on Creation Records, was a significant influence on the sound of Sloan's album "Smeared," contributing to its loud guitar aesthetic. "like my bloody Valentine and ride and all those sort of noisy pop bands that were on creation records and everything."

xref.title: Influence on "Twice Removed"
xref.body: Fleetwood Mac was among the artists Sloan members were listening to while creating "Twice Removed," contributing to the album's shift towards a quieter, more poppy sound. "I think some of the records that we're listening to more were like Fleetwood Mac or the third Velvet Underground album, which is sort of quieter records, you know."

xref.title: Influence on Modern Bands
xref.body: Big Star's innovative sound influenced a wide range of bands, from The Cars and Blondie to Sloan and Blink-182, solidifying their legacy as foundational figures in Powerpop. "Someone from the cars in Blondie to Sloan and Blink 1.2 were influenced by Big Star."

xref.title: Key A&R in Sloan's Discovery
xref.body: Cam Carpenter, an A&R representative at MCA Canada (before it became Universal), was an initial point of contact for Sloan. He received their demo tape, saw them play, and recommended them to Rick Arboit, thereby initiating the sequence of events that led to Sloan's major label deal. "I found the name of this guy, Cam Carpenter, who used to do ANR at MCA here in Canada back before it was universal."

"unless you were going to gigs at places like King Tutzer Wabahutzer or Sloan's or the Cathouse or the old fruit market, you've never heard of bands like Corelia or Yummie Fur or Embryo or 10P Invaders."

xref.body: Moe Berg is a member of "The High Women," an on-again, off-again Canadian indie supergroup that also includes Chris Murphy of Sloan, Craig Northe of Odds, and Steven Page, formerly of Barenaked Ladies. "He's also part of an on-again, off-again Canadian indie supergroup called The High Women, with Chris Murphy of Sloan, Craig Northe of Odds, and Steve Page, ex of the Bearnick and Ladies."

xref.title: Notable Contributors to Music
xref.body: Over the years, Jackalope's music featured contributions from a range of distinguished artists, including members of Sloan and Monster Magnet, Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails (who also co-produced), Alex Lifeson of Rush, and the three members named Don from Sons of Freedom. "Over the next few years, a number of really interesting artists contributed to Jackalope's music. The members of Sloan, the members of Monster Magnet, Trent Resner of Nine-H nails acted as a co-producer for a while. Alex Lifeson of Rush, and like I said, the three Don's from Sons of Freedom."

xref.title: Pre-Sloan Halifax Band
xref.body: Carney Lake Road was an obscure pre-Sloan band from the Halifax area, featuring Jay Ferguson and Chris Murphy, who had been playing together since age seven. They gained early excitement from an appearance on "Indie Street" on Much Music, which aired at 3 AM on Sunday nights, after performing at venues like the Rivoli. "Starting with a group called Carney Lake Road. Very obscure. I don't expect anyone to know it. Jay and I were both in it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Pre-Sloan Influencers and Tourmates
xref.body: The Straight Jackets were a Bedford-based band (part of a "New Brunswick experience") that headlined tours with Carney Lake Road. Their bass player, Jason Larson, had the nickname "Sloan," which was later adopted by the band Sloan, who even featured his face on their debut EP cover. "Straight Jackets was what they were called. They had a record out. It was very exciting."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Pre-Sloan Roots Rock Ensemble
xref.body: Blackpool was a pre-Sloan "Roots Rock band" in which Chris Murphy played bass. He joined primarily to record with renowned producer Terry Brown, who was holding open recording sessions. The band practiced equal money splitting, a tradition later adopted by Sloan. "It was more kind of a Roots Rock band, but at the time I was still into hardcore basically."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Sloan's Manager During Hiatus Rumors
xref.body: Chip Sutherland was Sloan's band manager during the period of breakup rumors in 1995. He publicly explained that Geffen Records' perceived lack of promotion, Andrew Scott's move to Toronto, and the band's desire to exit their major label contract were contributing factors to the speculation. "Band manager Chip Sutherland says there's an element of truth to the rumors that the band feels that Geffen Records hasn't adequately promoted their album in the United States."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Studio Host for "Twice Removed"
xref.body: Lenny Kravitz owned the studio where Sloan recorded their album "Twice Removed." The studio was equipped with his analog board and "all that Beatles gear," which contributed to the album's sound. "But it was also sounds great and was made in Lenny Kravitz studio. It was all with his analog board. Yeah, with all that Beatles gear and all that stuff."

xref.title: Young Halifax Talent Supported by Sloan
xref.body: Thrush Hermit was a band from the Halifax scene, featuring members like a young Joel Plaskett (around 16 years old). Sloan provided them with an opportunity to release a record through Murder Records and brought them on tour, offering support to emerging talent. "Thrusher mitt. Who gives you Joe Plasket now. Those guys were kids. They were 16 or whatever. And we, whatever, I don't know how much we had to do with their thing. But they were just young kids and we gave them an opportunity maybe to put out a record that they might not otherwise had."
